title: Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017
short_title: Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017

divisions.question: The majority voted against a motion that would have amended the normal [second reading](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html) motion, which is *that the bill be read for a second time*. Agreeing to read a bill for a second time is parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill. After this vote, the House can discuss the bill in more detail. The amendment to the normal second reading motion was introduced by Labor MP [Joel Fitzgibbon](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/hunter/joel_fitzgibbon). ### What was the amendment? > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House notes that a distracted Turnbull Government has failed to implement effective policies in a timely manner to ensure that Australian agriculture is achieving its full potential."* ### What was this bill all about? Read more about the [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5986) in its [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd068).

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: The coalition government moved the Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 to finalise country-of-origin labelling reforms, requiring all applicable food to comply with the new standard from 1 July 2018. The bill amends the Imported Food Control Act 1992 to allow authorised officers to enforce labelling requirements for imported food at the border, citing that 74% of Australians want to identify food origin and 73% supported labelling changes.

speeches.speaker: Joel Fitzgibbon
speeches.brief: The member moved a second reading amendment stating the Turnbull Government had failed to implement effective agriculture policies in a timely manner, and argued the bill was a minor change while country-of-origin labelling reforms were a distraction from the hepatitis A outbreak linked to imported frozen berries. He criticised the government for abolishing the Standing Council on Primary Industries, inaction on drought and biosecurity, and deterring foreign investment.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Broad
speeches.brief: The Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 was supported, arguing that country-of-origin labelling benefits health, local jobs, community and the environment, and citing that 87 per cent of Australians live within 50 kilometres of the coast. The Australian Made, Australian Grown logo (green triangle with kangaroo) was endorsed, free trade agreements with Korea, China, Japan and the Trans-Pacific Partnership were cited as supporting policy, and the previous shutdown of the live cattle industry was contrasted unfavourably with this approach.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: The member argued the Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 is a simple legislative change to enforce new country-of-origin labelling standards for imported food at the border, ensuring consumers can clearly distinguish Australian products. The bill shifts regulation from the Food Standards Code to Australian Consumer Law, with no additional costs for importers, and was supported by consultation with trading partners and stakeholders.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government has failed Australian agriculture through inadequate biosecurity, non-tariff barriers (e.g., India’s 40% tariff on chickpeas), labour shortages, climate change inaction, water infrastructure neglect, and poor telecommunications, while the Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 is only a minor tinkering.

speeches.speaker: Justine Keay
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the member for Hunter's amendment to the Imported Food Control Amendment Bill 2017, criticising the government's agricultural record, particularly the 2016 dairy crisis caused by Murray Goulburn and Fonterra's clawback practices, and the government's failure to act, instead offering only concessional loans that burdened farmers with debt. The speaker also noted that the then Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Agriculture ignored an invitation to visit Tasmanian dairy farmers.

speeches.speaker: Justine Keay
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that federal and Tasmanian Liberal governments have failed Tasmanian farmers through inaction on dairy, water infrastructure, export markets, labour shortages, and biosecurity, citing specific failures such as the lack of a blueberry export protocol with China and budget cuts to Biosecurity Tasmania. They noted that Labor's irrigation program involved $310 million in public-private investment and that Labor committed $5.7 million to boost biosecurity, a move welcomed by the Tasmanian Farmers and Graziers Association.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 is meaningless and purposeless, criticising Labor and the Greens for lacking a vision for agriculture. He defended the coalition's record on country-of-origin labelling, agricultural income turnaround, Inland Rail funding, the Regional Investment Corporation, and water infrastructure, while calling for reform of the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act to restore farmers' rights.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: The speech supported the Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 and the Labor amendment criticising the Turnbull government’s agricultural policies, citing $18 billion in imported food in 2015-16, a 20% increase from two years earlier, 608 food recalls from 2007-2017, and inadequate border inspections. It argued the government neglects horticultural and non-National Party farmers, and that free trade agreements are not essential for agricultural exports.

speeches.speaker: Kevin Hogan
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 is needed to give Australian consumers clear labelling so they can choose homegrown products, citing examples like Norco dairy, the Northern Co-operative Meat Company, and local blueberry farms in their electorate. They stated the bill does not ban imports but will benefit consumers and the agricultural sector.

speeches.speaker: David Littleproud
speeches.brief: The Imported Food Control Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2017 makes country-of-origin labelling compulsory from 1 July 2018, requiring a bar graph showing the proportion of Australian content; the speaker noted that 74% of Australians support identifying origin and that agricultural production reached $63.4 billion in 2016–17, with exports at nearly $49 billion.
